title: Flow Matching Calibration for Simulation-Based Inference under Model Misspecification
one_liner: Train a posterior estimator on abundant simulator data, then use a small set of real calibration pairs to transport its predictions toward the true posterior when the simulator is wrong.
lead: Simulation-based inference, meaning estimation of hidden scientific settings by learning from simulated observations, estimates unknown parameters, meaning the hidden scientific settings we want to recover, in scientific models by learning from synthetic data generated by a simulator. This works well when the simulator, the prior, meaning the assumed weighted set of parameter values before seeing data, and the observation noise all match reality closely. In practice they often do not. Small errors in the simulator or prior can make the learned posterior, meaning the weighted set of parameter values after seeing the observation, both biased and overconfident. FMCPE addresses that mismatch without discarding the original simulator-trained estimator. First it trains a standard posterior approximator on large simulated datasets. Then it uses flow matching, meaning direct training of a transport field that moves samples from one distribution, meaning one weighted set of candidate parameter values, to another along continuous paths, to correct those posterior predictions using a much smaller calibration set drawn from the real data-generating process. The correction step does not need to know which part of the simulator is wrong. It only needs examples of how simulator-trained posteriors should be nudged toward reality.

problem.h2: Simulation-based inference fails when the simulator is slightly wrong
paras: In simulation-based inference, you sample parameters, run a simulator, observe synthetic data, and train a model to invert that process. The output is a posterior, meaning a distribution over parameters after seeing the observation.

The method depends on a match between simulator and reality. If the simulator omits a physical effect, if the assumed noise is too small, or if the prior over parameters is misplaced, the learned posterior can become biased and too narrow. More simulated data does not fix that. It only teaches the model the wrong world more accurately.

callout.html: Learn the main posterior from large simulated data, then learn a transport that shifts that posterior toward the true one using a small calibration set from reality.

steps.text: Use abundant simulated data to train a posterior predictor for parameters given observations.
Obtain a much smaller set of real or trusted observation-parameter examples that reflect the true data-generating process.
For each calibration observation, draw parameter samples from the simulator-trained posterior estimator.
Train a flow-matching correction that moves those samples toward the true parameter distribution implied by the calibration set.
At test time, run the base estimator and then transport its samples through the learned correction field.

paras: The paper changes the target of the second-stage learning problem. Instead of retraining the full inference pipeline or explicitly modeling every source of simulator error, it learns a transport from the simulator posterior to the true posterior using calibration data.

hidden.name: posterior discrepancy field (the direction each simulator-posterior sample should move to match the true posterior)
paras: Misspecification does not only shift the posterior mean. It can also distort spread, skew, and local mass. FMCPE therefore learns a vector field, where vector field means a direction and speed of movement assigned to every sample location, that maps the simulator posterior toward the real one.

Flow matching learns that field by supervising continuous transport paths between source and target samples. The small calibration set is enough when the main simulator posterior is already close, because the correction only needs to learn the discrepancy, not the entire inference problem from scratch.

heat.caption: Darker cells mark regions where the base posterior needs stronger correction to align with calibrated reality.

reads.html: For each candidate parameter value, ask how far and in what direction it should move so the whole distribution matches what real calibration data imply.
FMCPE learns a flow-matching transport from simulator posterior samples to calibrated target samples, so the correction acts on the posterior discrepancy rather than the full simulator.

mechanism.h2: Why a transport correction can fix misspecified SBI
paras: The base simulator-trained estimator still contains most of the useful inference structure. It knows how observations relate to parameters in the approximate world described by the simulator. Throwing that away would waste a large amount of computation and synthetic coverage.

The real problem is the gap between approximate and true posterior. Flow matching targets exactly that gap. It learns a continuous correction map because the calibration set tells the method where simulator posterior samples should end up under reality. This is more data-efficient than relearning the full posterior, because the correction problem has smaller scope whenever the simulator is already close.

The corrected posterior becomes better calibrated because the transport adjusts both location and uncertainty. If the base posterior is too narrow, the flow can spread samples out. If it is shifted, the flow can move the mass. If only some regions are wrong, the vector field can vary locally. That flexibility is why the method handles unknown forms of misspecification without explicit simulator editing.

stages.s: simulator-trained posterior estimator plus small calibration set
learn discrepancy transport by flow matching

math.words: learn a velocity field whose value along an interpolation path matches the target direction from simulator-posterior samples toward calibrated posterior samples
math.equation: L_flow = E_(z_t, t)[ || v_theta(z_t, t, x) - u_t ||^2 ]
symbols: a parameter sample at interpolation time t along the transport path
the interpolation time between source and target distributions
the learned correction field parameterized by theta
the target transport direction at time t
the training loss for matching the correction field to the desired movement

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose the base posterior for one observation puts a parameter sample at 1.2, while the calibration target for that path is 1.8.
Halfway along the interpolation path, the desired direction is +0.6.
If the learned field predicts +0.5 there, the squared error is (0.5 - 0.6)^2 = 0.01.
If another sample should move -0.4 but the field predicts -0.1, its squared error is 0.09.
Training reduces these errors across many paths, so future samples are moved by a field that approximates the calibrated posterior transport.

math.note: The field does not need to explain the simulator bug directly. It only needs to produce the right posterior movement implied by calibration data.

charts.title: Simulator-trained posterior only
charts.note: The base estimator uses abundant simulation well, but posterior quality remains poor under misspecification because the synthetic world is wrong in a systematic way.

charts.title: FMCPE corrected posterior
charts.note: A modest calibration set yields a large gain because the flow stage corrects the posterior discrepancy instead of relearning the entire simulator-to-parameter map.

items.b: Calibration data are too sparse or unrepresentative.
items.html: If the real calibration set covers only a tiny corner of observation space, the learned correction field will not generalize. Future observations outside that region may still inherit the simulator's bias.

items.b: The base posterior is far from reality.
items.html: The two-stage approach assumes the simulator posterior is a useful starting point. If misspecification is severe, the transport problem becomes too large and the small calibration set may be insufficient.

items.b: The flow model is too weak.
items.html: A low-capacity correction field cannot reshape complicated posterior errors such as multimodal shifts or highly local spread changes.
Use a calibration set that spans the intended operating region, check how close the base posterior already is, and size the flow model to the complexity of the observed discrepancy.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Choose a small scientific simulator where controlled misspecification can be injected, such as wrong observation noise or a missing drift term. Train a standard simulation-based posterior estimator on abundant simulated data. Then generate a small calibration set from the true system and train the flow-matching correction.

Compare posterior bias, coverage, and sharpness before and after correction. It is important to visualize both the raw posterior samples and the transported samples so the shift in uncertainty is visible, not only the change in mean error.
demo.metric_eq: coverage_error = | measured credible-interval coverage - nominal coverage |
demo.closing: The demo should show that the correction works because it learns how the posterior must move under real data, even when the source of misspecification is unknown.
